notes: Louisiana localization of the civic-leadership legacy model carried in the Education OS app (the Willie L. Brown Jr. Institute Track, app iterations v28-v30, and its v29 state-localization template: capital, legislature, parish unit, standards framework, civic seal, anchor-industry hub, placement ladder, fellowship partner). DISCLAIMER, carried over from the app verbatim in spirit: this track is a proposal built from the Willie L. Brown Jr. Institute of Politics and Public Service's public mission and the Fellowship Program at San Francisco State University. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or reviewed by the Institute, SF State, or Mayor Brown. A named track would be offered under a partnership agreement and the Institute's review of every course. Louisiana civic-seal status: verify (marked per the v29 convention). 5 tracks x 10 themes x 5 grade bands = 250 blocks. Expanded by tools/generate_pack.py.

tracks.name: Public service as a craft: the Louisiana ladder

themes.theme: Service is a profession, not a slogan
themes.description: The legacy principle taught as craft: public service as roles, crews, evidence and credentials, always ending in front of a real audience.
themes.transfer_check: Complete one small act of documented public service in your parish and present it to a real audience beyond your classroom or family.

bands.K–2: Do one helpful job for the class or the school — water the garden, tidy the library corner — and tell the class what you did.
bands.3–5: Plan and do one small act of service for your school or street, keep a photo or note as evidence, and present it to another class.
bands.6–8: Complete one documented act of public service in your parish — a cleanup, a food drive shift — and present it to an audience beyond your class.
bands.9–10: Complete one small act of documented public service in your parish and present it to a real audience beyond your classroom or family.
bands.11–12: Design, lead and document an act of public service with a crew of younger learners, and present it to a parish body or community group.

themes.theme: The public servants two streets away
themes.description: Mapping who serves the public within walking distance — the librarian, the clerk, the firefighter, the extension agent — and what each actually does all day.
themes.transfer_check: Interview one working public servant in your parish about a typical day and present their actual duties against what you had assumed.

bands.K–2: Meet a helper who works for everyone — the librarian, the firefighter, the crossing guard — and draw what they do.
bands.3–5: Visit or write to one public worker in your town, ask what a day is like, and tell the class three things they really do.
bands.6–8: Interview one working public servant in your parish about a typical day and compare their real duties with what you had assumed.
bands.9–10: Interview one working public servant in your parish about a typical day and present their actual duties against what you had assumed.
bands.11–12: Interview two public servants in different offices, compare their days, and write the job-shadow guide a younger learner could use to meet them.

themes.theme: Who is missing from the room
themes.description: Inclusion as a design decision: reading any civic room — a board, a jury, a hearing — for who is absent and what kept them out.
themes.transfer_check: Observe one real public meeting and report who was present, who was affected but absent, and one barrier that plausibly explains the gap.

bands.K–2: Look around a class meeting and say who did not get a turn to speak.
bands.3–5: Watch a school or club meeting and write down who was there, who it was about but not there, and one reason why.
bands.6–8: Observe one real public meeting in person or online and report who was present, who was affected but absent, and one likely barrier.
bands.9–10: Observe one real public meeting and report who was present, who was affected but absent, and one barrier that plausibly explains the gap.
bands.11–12: Observe two public meetings, document the absences with evidence, and propose one change to time, place or notice that would close the gap.

themes.theme: The placement: hands inside a real agency
themes.description: The fellowship principle at every age — junior placements, shadow days and supervised hours inside parish offices, libraries and programs.
themes.transfer_check: Complete a placement, shadow day or structured volunteer shift with a real public body in your parish, with a supervisor's confirmation of what you did.

bands.K–2: Spend a morning helping at the school office or library with an adult, and say what job you did.
bands.3–5: Do a helper shift at the library, the school office or a community centre, with a grown-up's note saying what you did.
bands.6–8: Complete a shadow day or a structured volunteer shift with a real public body in your parish, with a supervisor's confirmation.
bands.9–10: Complete a placement, shadow day or structured volunteer shift with a real public body in your parish, with a supervisor's confirmation of what you did.
bands.11–12: Complete a multi-day placement in a parish office or program, keep a daily log, and present what the office actually does to your cohort.

themes.description: The weekly cohort habit: bringing what you saw in the field to a circle that questions it — reflection as part of the work, not a break from it.
themes.transfer_check: Run or take a speaking role in a seminar circle on a live local issue, presenting field evidence and taking questions on it.

bands.K–2: Sit in a circle and tell the class one thing you saw a helper do this week, then listen to a friend's.
bands.3–5: Bring one thing you saw in your town to a class circle, say it in two sentences, and answer one question about it.
bands.6–8: Take a speaking role in a seminar circle on a live local issue, presenting one piece of field evidence and taking questions.
bands.9–10: Run or take a speaking role in a seminar circle on a live local issue, presenting field evidence and taking questions on it.
bands.11–12: Run the seminar circle for a cohort across a term, set the questions, and keep the record of what the circle decided to go and see.

themes.description: The legacy chain: being mentored by someone ahead of you and mentoring someone behind you, with the leader's-story interview as a core text.
themes.transfer_check: Record a leader's-story interview with an experienced public servant or community elder, and lead one session passing a skill to a younger learner.

bands.K–2: Ask an older person to tell you about their job when they were young, and teach a younger child one thing you can do.
bands.3–5: Interview a grown-up about a time they helped their community, and lead one activity for younger children.
bands.6–8: Record a leader's-story interview with a community elder or public servant, and lead one session passing a skill to a younger learner.
bands.9–10: Record a leader's-story interview with an experienced public servant or community elder, and lead one session passing a skill to a younger learner.
bands.11–12: Record and edit a leader's-story interview for a public archive with consent, and mentor one younger learner through a full theme.

themes.description: First-generation pathways and the blocked door as history, law and practice — from segregated schoolrooms to the speaker's chair, with the debate included, not avoided.
themes.transfer_check: Research one Louisianan who broke a civic ceiling, and identify one current barrier data shows still standing in your parish, with the numbers.

bands.K–2: Hear the story of a Louisianan who did something they were told they could not, and draw the moment.
bands.3–5: Read about one Louisianan who broke a barrier and write what door was closed and how it opened.
bands.6–8: Research one Louisianan who broke a civic ceiling and find one barrier that public data shows still standing in your parish.
bands.9–10: Research one Louisianan who broke a civic ceiling, and identify one current barrier data shows still standing in your parish, with the numbers.
bands.11–12: Research the ceiling-breaker and the current barrier, present both sides of the debate about the barrier honestly, and propose one lawful step against it.

themes.theme: The stipend question: who can afford to serve
themes.description: Why unpaid service filters who serves — stipends, scheduling and the economics of showing up, taken seriously as program design.
themes.transfer_check: Cost out what four weeks of a real volunteer or placement role would require, and propose the support that would let a working student hold it.

bands.K–2: Talk about why some helpers get paid and some do not, and who could not come if it was not paid.
bands.3–5: Work out what it costs a family for a child to join a weekly club — time, travel, snacks — and say who could not afford it.
bands.6–8: Cost out what four weeks of a real volunteer role would require of a student, and propose one support that would let a working student hold it.
bands.9–10: Cost out what four weeks of a real volunteer or placement role would require, and propose the support that would let a working student hold it.
bands.11–12: Cost out the placement, propose the stipend or schedule, and draft the request to the office or funder who could provide it.

themes.description: The service ledger: hours, artifacts, references and credentials as a portfolio that opens doors — evidence, not testimony.
themes.transfer_check: Assemble your own service ledger to date — dated entries, artifacts, one verifiable reference — in a form a scholarship or employer could check.

bands.K–2: Keep a helper's chart with a sticker for each job you did and the date.
bands.3–5: Keep a service notebook — date, what you did, who saw it — for one term, and show it to your family.
bands.6–8: Assemble your own service ledger to date — dated entries, artifacts, one reference — in a form a scholarship could check.
bands.9–10: Assemble your own service ledger to date — dated entries, artifacts, one verifiable reference — in a form a scholarship or employer could check.
bands.11–12: Assemble the ledger, have a reference confirm one entry in writing, and submit it with a real scholarship, program or job application.

themes.theme: The on-ramp: from parish hall to public life
themes.description: The grade-12 fellowship principle localized: public-affairs programs, apprenticeships, civil service exams and the first paid public job in Louisiana.
themes.transfer_check: Map three real next-step routes into Louisiana public service for yourself or a case-study senior — requirements, deadlines, first application step completed or drafted.

bands.K–2: Name a public job you might like one day and one thing you would need to learn for it.
bands.3–5: Find out what a person has to do to get one public job in your parish — the school, the test, the first step.
bands.6–8: Map three real next-step routes into Louisiana public service for a case-study senior — requirements, deadlines, first step.
bands.9–10: Map three real next-step routes into Louisiana public service for yourself or a case-study senior — requirements, deadlines, first application step completed or drafted.
bands.11–12: Map three routes for yourself, complete the first application step of one for real, and write the timeline to the first paid public role.

tracks.name: The parish: government closest to the door

themes.description: Why Louisiana counts in parishes, where yours sits among the sixty-four, and what a parish is actually responsible for.
themes.transfer_check: Produce the one-page profile of your own parish — population, seat, governing form, and three services it actually runs — from official sources.

bands.K–2: Find your parish on a Louisiana map and say its name and its big town.
bands.3–5: Make a one-page picture profile of your parish — its seat, how many people, three things the parish does for you.
bands.6–8: Produce the one-page profile of your parish — population, seat, governing form, three services it runs — from official sources.
bands.9–10: Produce the one-page profile of your own parish — population, seat, governing form, and three services it actually runs — from official sources.
bands.11–12: Produce the profile for your parish and a neighbouring one from official sources, and explain one difference in what each runs and why.

themes.description: The two shapes of parish government — the traditional police jury and the home-rule charter with president and council — and how to tell which one governs you.
themes.transfer_check: Determine your parish's actual form of government from its charter or code, and diagram who holds executive and legislative power there.

bands.K–2: Learn the name of the group of grown-ups who run your parish.
bands.3–5: Find out whether your parish has a police jury or a president and council, and draw who is in charge.
bands.6–8: Determine your parish's form of government from its charter or code, and diagram who holds executive and legislative power.
bands.9–10: Determine your parish's actual form of government from its charter or code, and diagram who holds executive and legislative power there.
bands.11–12: Diagram your parish's form from its charter and compare it with a parish of the other form, showing one decision that would travel a different path in each.

themes.theme: The elected row: sheriff, clerk, assessor
themes.description: Louisiana's independently elected parish officers — sheriff, clerk of court, assessor, coroner — and why each answers to voters, not the council.
themes.transfer_check: List your parish's actual elected officers by name and office, and explain one real recent decision each office made that touched residents.

bands.K–2: Learn the name of your parish's sheriff and what a sheriff does.
bands.3–5: List your parish's sheriff, clerk of court and assessor by name, and say one thing each does for people.
bands.6–8: List your parish's elected officers by name and office, and explain one recent decision each made that touched residents.
bands.9–10: List your parish's actual elected officers by name and office, and explain one real recent decision each office made that touched residents.
bands.11–12: List the officers, attend or review one office's public report, and write the citizen's guide to what each office can and cannot do for a resident.

themes.theme: The school board and the schoolhouse
themes.description: Parish school boards as the education government: districts, superintendents, budgets and the meeting where your school's fate is set.
themes.transfer_check: Attend or watch one real school board meeting in your parish and report one decision made, who voted how, and who it affects.

bands.K–2: Learn that a group of elected grown-ups decides things about your school, and name one thing they decide.
bands.3–5: Find out who is on your parish school board and what they decided at their last meeting.
bands.6–8: Watch one real school board meeting in your parish and report one decision made, how the vote went, and who it affects.
bands.9–10: Attend or watch one real school board meeting in your parish and report one decision made, who voted how, and who it affects.
bands.11–12: Attend a school board meeting, report the decision, and write the two-paragraph brief a parent would need to speak on the item next time.

themes.theme: The special districts nobody can name
themes.description: Levee, drainage, water, fire, library and port districts — the boards that tax and decide, largely unwatched.
themes.transfer_check: Identify three special districts that cover your own address, and for one of them find its board, budget and next public meeting.

bands.K–2: Learn that different groups look after the water, the fire truck and the library where you live.
bands.3–5: Find out which district looks after your water and your fire protection, and who sits on its board.
bands.6–8: Identify two special districts that cover your own address and, for one of them, find its board and its next public meeting.
bands.9–10: Identify three special districts that cover your own address, and for one of them find its board, budget and next public meeting.
bands.11–12: Identify the districts, attend one board meeting, and report what it taxed and decided in words a neighbour would understand.

themes.theme: The parish budget, followed to the pothole
themes.description: Where parish money comes from — millages, sales taxes, fees — and following one line of it to a visible outcome on your street.
themes.transfer_check: From your parish's actual budget, trace one revenue source to one service, and check the service's condition where you live.

bands.K–2: Learn that the parish pays for the roads and the library with money from everyone, and find one thing it paid for on your street.
bands.3–5: Follow one thing the parish pays for — the library, a road — from where the money comes to what you can see.
bands.6–8: From your parish's budget, trace one revenue source to one service, and check the service's condition where you live.
bands.9–10: From your parish's actual budget, trace one revenue source to one service, and check the service's condition where you live.
bands.11–12: Trace two revenue lines to two services, compare their condition with what was budgeted, and write the question you would put to the council.

themes.theme: The permit, the complaint, the record
themes.description: The citizen's three transactions with the parish — asking permission, reporting a problem, requesting a record — done correctly.
themes.transfer_check: Complete one real parish transaction (permit lookup, service request, or public-records request) through the official channel and document the outcome.

bands.K–2: Learn the three things people ask the parish for — may I, please fix, may I see — and practise asking one politely.
bands.3–5: With an adult, report one real problem — a broken light, a pothole — through the parish's channel and follow what happens.
bands.6–8: Complete one real parish transaction — a permit lookup, a service request or a records request — through the official channel and document the outcome.
bands.9–10: Complete one real parish transaction (permit lookup, service request, or public-records request) through the official channel and document the outcome.
bands.11–12: Complete all three transactions for real, document each outcome and its timing, and write the guide that tells a resident how to do each.

themes.description: The open-meetings rules, the sign-up card, the three minutes — speaking to a parish body so it enters the record and moves someone.
themes.transfer_check: Deliver (or fully rehearse to the real rules) a three-minute public comment to a parish body on a live agenda item, structured for the record.

bands.K–2: Practise saying one clear sentence to a grown-up in charge about something you want changed.
bands.3–5: Write and say a one-minute comment to a class or school council about a real thing you want changed.
bands.6–8: Rehearse a three-minute public comment to a parish body on a live agenda item, to the real rules, structured for the record.
bands.9–10: Deliver (or fully rehearse to the real rules) a three-minute public comment to a parish body on a live agenda item, structured for the record.
bands.11–12: Deliver a public comment for real, obtain the record of it, and coach one other resident through delivering theirs.

themes.theme: Municipality and parish: who does what
themes.description: Cities, towns and villages inside parishes — mayors and councils versus parish government, and the services that switch at the city limit.
themes.transfer_check: For your own address, produce the who-fixes-what card: five common problems each matched to the correct government and office.

bands.K–2: Learn that the town and the parish are different, and say which one picks up the rubbish where you live.
bands.3–5: Make a card for five common problems — a pothole, a stray dog, a water leak — and say whether the town or the parish fixes each.
bands.6–8: For your own address, produce the who-fixes-what card: five common problems matched to the correct government and office.
bands.9–10: For your own address, produce the who-fixes-what card: five common problems each matched to the correct government and office.
bands.11–12: Produce the card for two addresses on either side of a city limit, and write the explanation of where the services switch and why.

themes.description: Escalation beyond the parish — state oversight, the legislative auditor, the courts and the press — the accountability ladder above local government.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real or case-study parish failure and map its escalation ladder in order, drafting the first escalation document.

bands.K–2: Learn who to tell when the grown-up in charge does not fix a problem.
bands.3–5: Put the steps in order for what a person does when the parish does not fix something — ask again, ask higher, ask the paper.
bands.6–8: Take one real or case-study parish failure and map its escalation ladder in order, drafting the first escalation letter.
bands.9–10: Take one real or case-study parish failure and map its escalation ladder in order, drafting the first escalation document.
bands.11–12: Map the ladder for a real failure, send or file the first escalation for real where appropriate, and document the response.

tracks.name: Baton Rouge: the Legislature and the law

themes.theme: The capitol and the two chambers
themes.description: The Louisiana Legislature — House and Senate, districts and leadership — and finding the two people who represent your own address.
themes.transfer_check: Identify your actual state representative and senator by district lookup, and summarise one bill each has authored or sponsored recently.

bands.K–2: Learn that Louisiana's laws are made in Baton Rouge by people the grown-ups voted for.
bands.3–5: Find the names of the two people who represent your home in Baton Rouge and one thing each cares about.
bands.6–8: Identify your state representative and senator by district lookup and summarise one bill each has authored recently.
bands.9–10: Identify your actual state representative and senator by district lookup, and summarise one bill each has authored or sponsored recently.
bands.11–12: Identify both, summarise a bill each, and write the one-page letter to one of them on a live issue, sent or ready to send.

themes.description: Regular sessions, fiscal sessions and special sessions — Louisiana's legislative rhythm and why timing decides what can pass.
themes.transfer_check: Find the current or most recent session's actual convening rules and dates, and explain what kinds of bills it could and could not take up.

bands.K–2: Learn that the law-makers meet at certain times of the year, like school terms.
bands.3–5: Find out when the Legislature meets this year and what kind of session it is.
bands.6–8: Find the current or most recent session's convening rules and dates, and explain what bills it could and could not take up.
bands.9–10: Find the current or most recent session's actual convening rules and dates, and explain what kinds of bills it could and could not take up.
bands.11–12: Compare a regular and a fiscal session's rules, and explain with a real example why a bill's timing decided whether it could pass.

themes.description: Filing, committee, floor, the other chamber, the governor's desk — following one real bill through the Louisiana process, including where bills go to die.
themes.transfer_check: Track one real bill from the current or last session through each stage on the Legislature's own website, and state where it stalled or how it became law.

bands.K–2: Put the picture cards in order: an idea, a vote, a signature, a law.
bands.3–5: Follow one real bill on the Legislature's website with an adult and colour in each stage it passed.
bands.6–8: Track one real bill from the current or last session through each stage on the Legislature's website, and state where it stalled or how it passed.
bands.9–10: Track one real bill from the current or last session through each stage on the Legislature's own website, and state where it stalled or how it became law.
bands.11–12: Track two bills on the same subject through the process, explain why one lived and one died, and write the memo a sponsor would need next session.

themes.theme: The committee room is the real floor
themes.description: Why testimony, amendment and death happen in committee — reading an agenda, watching a hearing, and the citizen's seat at the table.
themes.transfer_check: Watch one real committee hearing (live or archived) and report the arguments, the amendments, and the vote as the record shows them.

bands.K–2: Learn that small groups of law-makers talk about an idea first, before everyone votes.
bands.3–5: Watch a few minutes of a real committee hearing and say who spoke and what they asked for.
bands.6–8: Watch one real committee hearing, live or archived, and report the arguments, the amendments, and the vote as the record shows them.
bands.9–10: Watch one real committee hearing (live or archived) and report the arguments, the amendments, and the vote as the record shows them.
bands.11–12: Watch a hearing and write the testimony you would have given on the bill, in the form and time limit the committee allows.

themes.description: Louisiana's civil-law inheritance — codes over precedent in private law, and what that history means at the notary, the succession and the property line.
themes.transfer_check: Explain, with one concrete everyday example, how Louisiana's civil-law tradition treats a matter differently from a common-law state, verified against an authoritative source.

bands.K–2: Learn that Louisiana has some rules of its own that other states do not.
bands.3–5: Find one everyday thing Louisiana does differently from the state next door, and explain it in a sentence.
bands.6–8: Explain, with one everyday example, how Louisiana's civil-law tradition treats a matter differently from a common-law state, checked against a source.
bands.9–10: Explain, with one concrete everyday example, how Louisiana's civil-law tradition treats a matter differently from a common-law state, verified against an authoritative source.
bands.11–12: Explain two differences with sources, and interview a notary or clerk about how one of them shows up in a real transaction.

themes.description: Louisiana's long constitution and the amendments on nearly every ballot — reading the question, the fiscal note and the arguments before voting.
themes.transfer_check: Take one real past or pending constitutional amendment, translate its ballot language into plain words, and present the strongest case each way.

bands.K–2: Learn that the big rule book of the state can be changed by the grown-ups voting.
bands.3–5: Read one amendment question from an old ballot with an adult and say it in your own words.
bands.6–8: Take one real past or pending constitutional amendment, translate its ballot language into plain words, and give the case each way.
bands.9–10: Take one real past or pending constitutional amendment, translate its ballot language into plain words, and present the strongest case each way.
bands.11–12: Translate every amendment on a real ballot into plain words with the case each way, and publish the guide for voters in your parish.

themes.description: The state budget's shape — where Louisiana's money comes from and goes — and the offices that watch it, from the fiscal office to the legislative auditor.
themes.transfer_check: From official budget documents, chart the state's five largest spending areas and follow one of them down to a program operating in your parish.

bands.K–2: Learn that the state pays for schools, roads and hospitals, and name one thing near you it paid for.
bands.3–5: Make a picture chart of the biggest things the state spends money on, from a simple official page.
bands.6–8: From official budget documents, chart the state's five largest spending areas and follow one down to a program in your parish.
bands.9–10: From official budget documents, chart the state's five largest spending areas and follow one of them down to a program operating in your parish.
bands.11–12: Chart the spending, follow one line to your parish, and compare what the program received with what the budget said, with the auditor's report if there is one.

themes.theme: The agencies that carry out the words
themes.description: Departments, boards and the administrative code — how a passed law becomes a rule, a form and an inspector at the door.
themes.transfer_check: Pick one state rule that touches your life, find it in the administrative code, and trace it back to the statute that authorised it.

bands.K–2: Learn that after a rule is made, someone has to check it is followed — the inspector, the nurse, the officer.
bands.3–5: Find one rule that touches your life — the school bus, the swimming pool — and the office that checks it.
bands.6–8: Pick one state rule that touches your life — the school bus, the pool, the food truck — and find the agency and the code section that carry it out.
bands.9–10: Pick one state rule that touches your life, find it in the administrative code, and trace it back to the statute that authorised it.
bands.11–12: Trace the rule to its statute, find the last time it was amended and why, and write the plain-language explainer a business owner would need.

themes.description: The routes from resident to lawmaking: contacting your legislator, testifying in committee, and the idea that becomes a filed bill.
themes.transfer_check: Draft a one-page bill proposal on a real local problem and deliver it (or a rehearsed committee testimony for it) in proper form to the right office.

bands.K–2: Tell a grown-up in charge one thing you would change and why, in two sentences.
bands.3–5: Write a one-paragraph idea for a new rule at school and present it to the student council or the principal.
bands.6–8: Draft a one-page bill proposal on a real local problem and deliver a rehearsed committee testimony for it in proper form.
bands.9–10: Draft a one-page bill proposal on a real local problem and deliver it (or a rehearsed committee testimony for it) in proper form to the right office.
bands.11–12: Draft the proposal, deliver it to a legislator's office for real, and document what the office said it would need to file it.

themes.description: Louisiana's court ladder — district courts, courts of appeal, the Supreme Court — and how an ordinary case climbs it.
themes.transfer_check: Map one real Louisiana case's path through the court system from filing to final ruling, naming each court correctly.

bands.K–2: Learn that when people disagree about the rules, a judge decides, and that there are bigger courts above the first one.
bands.3–5: Put Louisiana's courts in order from the first court to the highest, with a picture for each.
bands.6–8: Map one real Louisiana case's path through the court system from filing to final ruling, naming each court.
bands.9–10: Map one real Louisiana case's path through the court system from filing to final ruling, naming each court correctly.
bands.11–12: Map two cases that reached different levels, explain why one stopped where it did, and attend or review one hearing at any level.

tracks.name: Elections, voice and the ballot in Louisiana

themes.description: Who may vote in Louisiana, the registration routes and deadlines, and the purge-proof habit of checking your own record.
themes.transfer_check: Verify a real registration (yours or a consenting adult's) through the state's official portal, and correct or complete one detail if needed.

bands.K–2: Learn that grown-ups sign up to vote and that you can sign up when you are older.
bands.3–5: Find out how a person registers to vote in Louisiana and the age they can pre-register.
bands.6–8: Verify a consenting adult's registration through the state's official portal and note what would need correcting.
bands.9–10: Verify a real registration (yours or a consenting adult's) through the state's official portal, and correct or complete one detail if needed.
bands.11–12: Verify your own registration or pre-registration, help two consenting adults check theirs, and write the yearly check-your-record reminder for a group.

themes.description: The majority-vote primary and the runoff — Louisiana's distinctive system, the reforms that keep changing it, and reading the current rules for any given office.
themes.transfer_check: For two different offices on the next real ballot, find and explain the election rules that currently govern each, citing the Secretary of State's guidance.

bands.K–2: Learn that when nobody gets more than half the votes, there is a second vote.
bands.3–5: Explain, with counters, what happens in Louisiana when no one gets more than half, and when there is a runoff.
bands.6–8: For two different offices on the next real ballot, find and explain the election rules that currently govern each.
bands.9–10: For two different offices on the next real ballot, find and explain the election rules that currently govern each, citing the Secretary of State's guidance.
bands.11–12: Explain the rules for three offices, trace the recent reform that changed one of them, and write the voter's one-page guide to which system applies where.

themes.description: Millages, propositions, judgeships and boards — the down-ballot lines that move your money and your parish, read before election day.
themes.transfer_check: Obtain your actual sample ballot for a real election and produce a plain-language voter guide for every line below the top race.

bands.K–2: Look at a sample ballot with an adult and count how many questions are on it besides the big race.
bands.3–5: Take a real sample ballot and, with help, say in your own words what two of the small questions would do.
bands.6–8: Obtain your parish's sample ballot for a real election and write a plain-language guide for three lines below the top race.
